entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Georg Fugger von der Lilie (1453–1506) was a German merchant of the Fugger dynasty.

Born in “in der Lilie’s Manor, Ulm, Duchy of Swabia (present-day Germany), Fugger rose to prominence as a trader and financier, leveraging the family’s extensive network of contacts and resources to accumulate vast wealth and influence.

Fugger’s most notable achievement was his role in financing the Habsburg Empire’s military campaigns, including the conquest of the Holy Roman Empire, and his strategic investments in the textile and mining industries.

His legacy extends to the modern era, as the Fugger dynasty continued to shape European politics and economy through the centuries, leaving an indelible mark on the continent.

The phrase “Fugger Effect” has been coined to describe the lasting impact of his business acumen and strategic thinking on the development of capitalism and modern industry.

Fugger’s impressive collection of precious gems, including the famous “Black Diamond,’ remains a testament to his exquisite taste and love of luxury.

Despite his significant influence, Fugger’s personal life remains somewhat of a mystery, with only a handful of contemporary accounts surviving to the present day.


Fugger's business partnerships with the Medicis and the Ottoman Empire contributed to the rich tapestry of international relations during the Renaissance.

Fugger's financial support of the Catholic Church helped to cement his position as a key player in European politics.

Fugger's rise to power was facilitated by his strategic marriages to the daughters of wealthy merchants and nobles.

Fugger's involvement in the textile industry helped to establish a thriving market for luxury goods in Europe.

Fugger's investments in the mining industry contributed to the development of new technologies and mining techniques.

Fugger's patronage of the arts and architecture helped to promote the development of Renaissance culture.
